https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/motherboard_marked.0aed3ba85f2806020b7c6cb582cc2da441107001353717c0c3989e971b230de0_hu_2f621adf180d92b6.webp 1111w"><img class="title-image" alt="Motherboard" width="1111" height="647" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/motherboard_marked.0aed3ba85f2806020b7c6cb582cc2da441107001353717c0c3989e971b230de0.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Motherboard with important parts labelled</figcaption></figure></div></figure><h3 class="tab-title">Diagram</h3><figure class="tab cover nested-single" id="cover-diagram"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/main.0637ddde78a568ef68ceee846c3474cabadfe0ee7950a44c640e07c8b13a887f.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/main.0637ddde78a568ef68ceee846c3474cabadfe0ee7950a44c640e07c8b13a887f_hu_3ee29669d3d0d833.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/main.0637ddde78a568ef68ceee846c3474cabadfe0ee7950a44c640e07c8b13a887f_hu_f9f3b5cc875a5ca0.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/main.0637ddde78a568ef68ceee846c3474cabadfe0ee7950a44c640e07c8b13a887f_hu_b3b3a00160c217a6.webp 2049w"><img class="title-image" alt="Diagram" width="2049" height="1027" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/main.0637ddde78a568ef68ceee846c3474cabadfe0ee7950a44c640e07c8b13a887f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption>Main architecture diagram<br>If you have trouble following the components: Top is only accessed by ARM9, bottom section is ARM7-only, middle section is shared.</figcaption></figure></div></section><hr><h2 id="a-quick-introduction">A quick introduction</h2><p>This console is an interesting answer to many needs that weren’t possible to fulfil in the handheld ecosystem. There will be some innovation and a few compromises, but this combination may pave the way for new and ingenious content.</p><hr><h2 id="cpu">CPU</h2><p>As with Nintendo’s <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/">previous portable console</a>, the system revolves around a big chip named <strong>CPU NTR</strong>. ‘NTR’ is shorthand for <strong>Nitro</strong>, the codename of the original Nintendo DS. This SoC is also the continuation of a prosperous <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#the-nintendo-partnership">Nintendo-ARM partnership</a>, which originally started with the Game Boy Advance.</p><p>Now, before we check out the new CPUs, let’s look at how ARM evolved during the late 90s, as this impacted the technology ultimately found inside the Nintendo DS.</p><h3 id="arms-new-territories">ARM’s new territories</h3><p>During the mid-90s, ARM was experiencing an influx of businesses from the mobile market (before cellphones became ‘smart’). Yet, it struggled to please a particular sector: <strong>high-performance computing</strong>. The ARM7 was enjoyed by many mobile devices, but it didn’t quite satisfy Apple (with its ‘Newton’ PDA line) and Acorn (with its RiscPC line), both of whom shipped software that could benefit from a faster CPU. Aside from the lack of a 64-bit solution (something <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#cpu">MIPS was already commercialising</a>), ARM was also unable to produce a CPU that operated faster than 40 MHz. Altogether, the bottlenecks were starting to pile up.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/dec_work.8078d9c1b5acb56474fc972ebe91814117811cc87cf61b8cb369671c32344552.webp"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/dec_work.8078d9c1b5acb56474fc972ebe91814117811cc87cf61b8cb369671c32344552.webp"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="705" height="950" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/dec_work.8078d9c1b5acb56474fc972ebe91814117811cc87cf61b8cb369671c32344552_hu_a3b558e6af858ed2.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">DEC’s ‘Digital Personal Workstation’ model 433au (1997), carrying an Alpha 21164A CPU.</figcaption></figure><p>Nevertheless, during the commercialisation of the ARM7 line, ARM had already started work on a successor called <strong>ARM8</strong>, the first attempt into the high-performance market. Coincidentally, <strong>Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC)</strong>, the American company historically famous for their line of PDP and VAX machines (the so-called ‘minicomputers’) along with the sophisticated VMS operating system, was experiencing an opposite problem: They struggled to deliver a low-power CPU based on their high-performance solutions.</p><p>Well, it so happened that <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-1-2-a-new-cpu-venture">ARM’s licensing model</a> turned into an opportunity for DEC, who chose to develop a new CPU by borrowing materials from ARM (its instruction set and microarchitecture).</p></div><p>In the end, DEC grabbed the datapath design of their RISC-based <strong>Alpha</strong> processor and, with the help of ARM, mixed it with ARM’s microarchitecture <sup id="bibref:1"><a href="#bib:cpu-jaggar" role="doc-biblioref">[1]</a></sup>. This collaboration led to the <strong>StrongARM</strong> CPU, which was released in 1996 and targeted the performance sector.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/strongarm.8edf135c42541116bf95a1964505f1e95870d25c6e6b13eb318c4e09b327b737.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/strongarm.8edf135c42541116bf95a1964505f1e95870d25c6e6b13eb318c4e09b327b737_hu_865fffa143907860.webp 450w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="450" height="388" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/strongarm.8edf135c42541116bf95a1964505f1e95870d25c6e6b13eb318c4e09b327b737.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">A 233 MHz StrongARM CPU, part of the CPU upgrade card offered for the Acorn RiscPC.</figcaption></figure><p>StrongARM was a new ARM-based CPU that featured <sup id="bibref:2"><a href="#bib:cpu-furber" role="doc-biblioref">[2]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>The <strong>ARMv4 instruction set</strong>. If you want to know more about it, I’ve <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#commanding-the-cpu">previously analysed it</a> in the Game Boy Advance article.</li><li>Up to <strong>233 MHz</strong> of clock speed, roughly 583% faster than the beefiest ARM7 chip.</li><li><strong>5-stage pipeline</strong>, an increment from the original <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-1-the-core">3-stage design</a>.</li><li>A <strong>new cache system</strong> implementing a <strong>Harvard architecture</strong>, where <strong>16 KB</strong> are allocated for instructions and another <strong>16 KB</strong> for data.<ul><li>This design helped alleviate memory bottlenecks (something the von Neumann/Princeton model suffered from).</li></ul></li></ul><p>It’s worth mentioning that this chip still managed to work with a <strong>3.3 V</strong> supply, like previous ARM chips. In fact, the StrongARM needs 2 Volts and only dissipates 1 W <sup id="bibref:3"><a href="#bib:cpu-furber" role="doc-biblioref">[3]</a></sup>. By contrast, Intel’s 200 MHz Pentium chip pulls 3.5 V and has a power dissipation of up to 15.5 W <sup id="bibref:4"><a href="#bib:cpu-pentium" role="doc-biblioref">[4]</a></sup>.</p><p>As expected, Acorn and Apple were so dazzled by the new chip that they immediately shipped CPU upgrades and further Newton models, respectively, using DEC’s invention.</p><p>In the same year, ARM also released their promised ARM8-based CPU, the ARM810. It was comparably slower and offered no practical advantages over the StrongARM. So, too little and too late resulted in no commercial interest. Consequently, ARM moved on to improving the ARM7 line for the mobile market. However, the potential of DEC’s CPU was so disruptive that ARM Holdings absorbed StrongARM’s design <sup id="bibref:5"><a href="#bib:cpu-jaggar" role="doc-biblioref">[5]</a></sup> to produce their next line of CPUs, the <strong>ARM9</strong> (which the Nintendo DS houses).</p><h4 id="turning-points">Turning points</h4><p>Thanks to the StrongARM, ARM also cemented its position in the handheld market, completely displacing <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#cpu">MIPS</a> and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/#cpu">SuperH</a> as viable alternatives. From then on, ARM was en route to become the most adopted architecture for mobile devices <sup id="bibref:6"><a href="#bib:cpu_android_abi" role="doc-biblioref">[6]</a></sup>.</p><p>Unfortunately for DEC, this CPU will be their last major achievement before being acquired by Compaq in 1998. The fate of StrongARM would then be in the hands of Intel, who continued development under the new ‘Intel XScale’ line… until they liquidated the division to focus on <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#p6-and-the-end-of-pentium-numbers">‘low-power’ x86 CPUs</a> (i.e. the Intel Atom) <sup id="bibref:7"><a href="#bib:cpu-xscale" role="doc-biblioref">[7]</a></sup>. 15 years later, not only Intel has lost its chance in the mobile market, but now they furiously find themselves running head-to-head against ARM in the desktop arena.</p><h3 id="nintendos-debuting-soc">Nintendo’s debuting SoC</h3><p>Aside from the aforementioned advancements, CPU NTR also bundles an interesting <strong>multi-processor architecture</strong> using two different ARM CPUs, the <strong>ARM7TDMI</strong> and the <strong>ARM946E-S</strong>. This design was done before ARM Holdings officially released <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-3ds/#cpu">multi-processor solutions</a>. So, their functioning may be considered a bit unorthodox (taking into account the present technology available).</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/cpu_ntr.e00a63784a027cf659e3c8d8f61868a1c9708a3f8b3d4b89e533e991218c0efb.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/cpu_ntr.e00a63784a027cf659e3c8d8f61868a1c9708a3f8b3d4b89e533e991218c0efb_hu_de39863ecfda036.webp 464w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="464" height="388" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/cpu_ntr.e00a63784a027cf659e3c8d8f61868a1c9708a3f8b3d4b89e533e991218c0efb.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The CPU NTR chip.</figcaption></figure><p>While this is not the first parallel system analysed for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/">this series</a>, its design is very different from the rest. For instance, we are not talking about the ‘experimental’ master-slave configuration that the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/sega-saturn/">Saturn</a> debuted or the ‘co-processor’ approach found on the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/">PS1</a> or <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/">N64</a>. The Nintendo DS includes two very independent computers that will perform exclusive operations, each one having a dedicated bus. This design methodology is called <strong>asymmetric multiprocessing</strong> and the resulting CPUs’ co-dependency will condition the overall performance of this console.</p><p>Let’s now take a look at the two CPUs.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-1-1-arm7tdmi-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-1-1-arm7tdmi">ARM7TDMI</a></li><li id="tab-1-2-arm946e-s-link"><a href="#tab-1-2-arm946e-s">ARM946E-S</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-1-1-arm7tdmi"><h4 id="tab-1-1-arm7tdmi" class="tab-title">ARM7TDMI</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/arm7_core.63b976b9d3d6767ceef0dacf94f0f531de1f3969d920ad41e8317a063caf6442.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="716" height="380" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/arm7_core.63b976b9d3d6767ceef0dacf94f0f531de1f3969d920ad41e8317a063caf6442.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">ARM7 structure and components.</figcaption></figure><p>Starting with the more familiar one, the <strong>ARM7TDMI</strong> is the same CPU found on the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#cpu">Game Boy Advance</a> but now running at <strong>~34 MHz</strong> (double its original speed). It still includes all its original features (especially <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-3-squeezing-performance">Thumb</a>).</p><p>Now for the changes: Because Nintendo’s engineers placed the ARM7 next to most of the I/O ports, this CPU will be tasked with arbitrating and assisting I/O operations. In fact, no other processor can directly connect to the I/O. As you can see, this is not the ‘main’ processor that will be in charge of the system, but rather the ‘sub-processor’ offloading the main CPU by passing data around many components.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-2-arm946e-s">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-2-arm946e-s"><h4 id="tab-1-2-arm946e-s" class="tab-title">ARM946E-S</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/arm9_core.fa4bbe6b32e4f285e48dae9fea642aacc4862da74cf0aebac8d956229e0e1f45.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="888" height="556" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/arm9_core.fa4bbe6b32e4f285e48dae9fea642aacc4862da74cf0aebac8d956229e0e1f45.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">ARM9 structure and components.</figcaption></figure><p>Here is the ‘main’ CPU of the Nintendo DS, the <strong>ARM946E-S</strong>. It runs at <strong>~67 MHz</strong>, so not exactly ‘StrongARM speed’. Yet, being part of the <strong>ARM9 series</strong>, this core in particular not only inherits all the features of the <strong>ARM7TDMI</strong> and <strong>StrongARM</strong>, but also includes some additional bits you may find interesting <sup id="bibref:8"><a href="#bib:cpu-arm9reference" role="doc-biblioref">[8]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>The <strong>ARMv5TE ISA</strong>, an extension of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#commanding-the-cpu">previous ARMv4 ISA</a> and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-3-squeezing-performance">Thumb</a>, including more instructions and a faster multiplier.<ul><li>If you take a look at the core name, the letter ‘E’ means <strong>Enhanced DSP</strong> which implies that lots of these new instructions have to do with applications for signal processing.</li><li>The extended Thumb is sometimes called <strong>Thumb v2</strong>. It adds <code>BLX</code> and <code>BKPT</code>, which assists the switching between ARM and Thumb mode; and facilitates debugging, respectively.</li></ul></li><li><strong>5-stage Pipeline</strong>, like the StrongARM and ARM8 line.</li><li><strong>12 KB of L1 Cache</strong>: The core now features cache (originally lacking in the ARM7TDMI) and, akin to the Hardvard-based StrongARM, <strong>8 KB</strong> are allocated for instructions and <strong>4 KB</strong> for data.<ul><li>The cache employs a <strong>write buffer</strong> mechanism where RAM is updated asynchronously, so the CPU can work on other tasks.</li></ul></li><li><strong>48 KB of Tightly-Coupled Memory</strong> or ‘TCM’: Similar to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#cpu">Scratchpad memory</a>. Although, this one discriminates between instructions (32 KB) and data (16 KB).</li><li>An integrated <strong>CP15 co-processor</strong>. It acts as a <strong>Memory Protection Unit (MPU)</strong>, stipulating which memory ranges can be accessed, cached and/or written to.</li></ul><p>Nintendo also added the following components around it:</p><ul><li>A <strong>Divider and Square root unit</strong> to speed up these types of operations, as the ARM9 by itself is not capable of performing this type of arithmetic.</li><li>A <strong>Direct Memory Access Controller</strong>: Accelerates memory transfers without depending on the CPU. Combined with the use of cache, both CPU and DMA can potentially work concurrently.<ul><li>Cache and DMA can provide a lot of performance but also create new problems, such as <strong>data integrity and coherence</strong>. So, programmers will have to manually maintain memory consistency by <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#preventing-past-mishaps">flushing the write buffer</a> before triggering DMA, for instance.</li></ul></li></ul><p>I guess with hardware like this, it’s easy to figure out the <em>real</em> reason kids loved this console, eh?</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-1-arm7tdmi">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="interconnection">Interconnection</h3><p>So far I’ve talked about how the two CPUs work individually. But to work as a whole, they are required to cooperate constantly. To accomplish this, both CPUs directly ‘talk’ to each other using a dedicated <strong>FIFO unit</strong> <sup id="bibref:9"><a href="#bib:cpu-double" role="doc-biblioref">[9]</a></sup>, this block of data holds two 64-byte queues (up to 16 elements) for <strong>bi-directional communication</strong>.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/fifo.c4d98c6137c2a13d5b38f40e496f477abb5e9369515025c2344a7fe55c7b3ae4.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="672" height="211" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/fifo.c4d98c6137c2a13d5b38f40e496f477abb5e9369515025c2344a7fe55c7b3ae4.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Representation of FIFO unit.</figcaption></figure><p>This works as follows: The ‘sender’ CPU (that effectively needs to send the other a message) places a 32-bit block of data in the queue, and the CPU acting as a ‘receiver’ can then pull that block from the queue and perform the required operations with it.</p><p>Whenever there’s a value written on the queue, either CPU can fetch it manually (<strong>polling</strong>) however, this requires constantly checking for new values (which can be expensive). Alternatively, an <strong>interrupt unit</strong> can be activated to notify the receiver whenever there’s a new value in the queue.</p><h3 id="main-memory">Main memory</h3><p>Just like its predecessor, RAM is spread around many different locations, enabling it to prioritise data placement by access rate. In summary, we have the following general-purpose memory available:</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/ram.21dcaebc6762aad7d4570883637def6e1b59bcedebdfff164a8a7bf8ac43099a.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="752" height="495" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/cpu/ram.21dcaebc6762aad7d4570883637def6e1b59bcedebdfff164a8a7bf8ac43099a.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">RAM model of this console.</figcaption></figure><ul><li><strong>32 KB of WRAM</strong> (Work RAM) using a <strong>32-bit</strong> bus: To hold fast data shared between the ARM7 and ARM9.<ul><li>Bear in mind that only one CPU can access the same address at a time.</li></ul></li><li><strong>64 KB of WRAM</strong> using a <strong>32-bit</strong> bus: For fast data as well, but only accessible from the ARM7, like the GBA had.</li><li><strong>4 MB of PSRAM</strong> using a <strong>16-bit</strong> bus: A slower type, available from either CPU and it’s controlled by a memory interface unit.<ul><li>Pseudo SRAM or ‘PSRAM’ is a variant of DRAM that, by contrast, performs refreshes from within the chip. Therefore, behaving like SRAM (the faster, but more expensive alternative to DRAM). This design reminds me of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#clever-memory-system">1T‑SRAM</a>.</li></ul></li></ul></div><h3 id="backwards-compatibility">Backwards compatibility</h3><p>Even though the architecture is significantly different from its predecessor, it still managed to maintain the critical bits that would grant it native compatibility with Game Boy Advance games.</p><p>But for the DS to revert to an ‘internal’ GBA, the former includes a set of software routines that set the console in <strong>AGB Compatibility Mode</strong>. In doing so, it effectively halts the ARM9, disables most of the ‘special’ hardware, redirects the buses, puts the ARM7 in charge and slows it down at 16.78 MHz. Finally, the ARM7 proceeds to boot the original AGB BIOS which bootstraps the GamePak cartridge (just like an original Game Boy Advance). This mode still exhibits some features not found in the original console, such as displaying the game with black margins (we’ll see in the next section that the new screen resolution happens to be bigger). Moreover, since the DS has two screens, users can set which screen will be used to display the GBA game.</p><p>Once in GBA mode <strong>there’s no going back</strong>, the console must be reset to re-activate the rest of the hardware.</p><h3 id="unused-power">Unused Power</h3><p>With so many sophisticated components fitted in a single and inexpensive chip, it’s no mystery that some issues emerged due to the way they were forced to work with each other.</p><p>Let me start with the ARM9, this CPU runs at twice the speed of the ARM7, but most (if not all) of the I/O depends on the ARM7. Thus, the ARM9 is vulnerable to excessive stalling until the ARM7 answers. If that wasn’t enough, <strong>ARM9’s external bus runs at half the speed</strong>, another bottleneck to add to the list.</p><p>Additionally, the Main Memory bus is only <strong>16-bit wide</strong>. Thus, whenever any CPU needs to fetch a word (32-bit wide) from memory, the interface <strong>stalls the CPU</strong>, using up to 3 ‘wait’ cycles, until a full word is reconstructed. The worst impact happens when memory access is not sequential, which makes it stall for every single access. This issue will also arise when instructions are fetched (unfortunately, ARM didn’t support sequential opcode fetching back then) which, to my dismay, also affects Thumb code (since every 16-bit fetch is done as a 32-bit block). On the other hand, this ‘penalty’, as some sources call it, can be alleviated by making full use of cache and TCM.</p><p>All in all, this means that in the worst case, the ARM9’s whopping 66 MHz horsepower is practically reduced to a mere ~8 MHz. That is if the program makes an abysmal use of cache and TCM.</p><p>For a detailed report, I recommend checking out Martin Korth’s document <sup id="bibref:10"><a href="#bib:cpu-korth" role="doc-biblioref">[10]</a></sup>, specifically, the ‘DS Memory Timings’ section.</p><hr><h2 id="graphics">Graphics</h2><p>This section is a bit unusual because not only this console has multiple screens to draw, but also a combination of traditional tile engines working alongside a modern renderer.</p><p>Let’s begin with the physical attributes: The Nintendo DS contains two LCD screens, each one being <strong>256x192 pixels</strong> wide, which is ~20% more pixels than the GBA. They can display 262,144 colours (18-bit) and refresh at ~60 Hz.</p><h3 id="architecture">Architecture</h3><p>The graphics subsystem can draw 2D and 3D objects. The former is composed of two-dimensional geometry that is filled with bitmaps of 8x8 pixels wide (called ‘tiles’), while the latter draws three-dimensional objects (polygons) using vertices.</p><p>Diving into the internal chip that operates those screens, we can observe this console has distinctive hardware for 2D and 3D geometry. The 2D data is operated by a familiar engine, the PPU (now just called <strong>2D engine</strong>), while 3D data is handled by a completely new subsystem. It’s worth mentioning that while this is not the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/">first console</a> to debut 3D graphics, it’s still the first one to include an in-house design to render 3D graphics.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/gpu/overall.c0eee206ada177ad2eb0dd22464879ea37c9d22167e0a8028b97ee2a59364d81.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="896" height="297" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/gpu/overall.c0eee206ada177ad2eb0dd22464879ea37c9d22167e0a8028b97ee2a59364d81.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Layout of the different graphic units.</figcaption></figure><p>Now, these engines must be linked to either screen, this is not an issue for 2D-only games since there’s one 2D engine for each screen. However, for those games who want to show off cutting-the-edge features, there’s only one 3D engine available. As a consequence, 3D capabilities are only available on one screen at a time. But what about mixing 2D and 3D objects? Absolutely, let me explain each engine separately so we can discuss this afterwards.</p><h3 id="constructing-a-frame-with-2d-graphics">Constructing a frame with 2D graphics</h3><p>Before we review each stage, I recommend reading a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#graphics">previous article</a> about the GBA’s PPU since here I’ll just mention the changes that construct the ‘next-gen’ of 2D games. Also, since there are two engines, the first one is named <strong>Main</strong> while the second one is called <strong>Sub</strong>. This doesn’t necessarily imply which screen is each one connected to. On the other side, ‘Main’ contains a bit more functions than ‘Sub’.</p><p>To help the explanations, this time I’m going to borrow the assets of <em>New Super Mario Bros</em>.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-2-1-tiles-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-2-1-tiles">Tiles</a></li><li id="tab-2-2-background-types-link"><a href="#tab-2-2-background-types">Background types</a></li><li id="tab-2-3-background-modes-link"><a href="#tab-2-3-background-modes">Background modes</a></li><li id="tab-2-4-sprites-link"><a href="#tab-2-4-sprites">Sprites</a></li><li id="tab-2-5-result-link"><a href="#tab-2-5-result">Result</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-2-1-tiles"><h4 id="tab-2-1-tiles" class="tab-title">Tiles</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/tiles.5230eed389fc325b50fd5a4f6a7074898328515856d0d9cf140323832b771d57.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="256" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/tiles.5230eed389fc325b50fd5a4f6a7074898328515856d0d9cf140323832b771d57.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Some tiles found in VRAM. For demonstration purposes, a default palette is used.</figcaption></figure><p>By now we all know how a basic tile system works, but how are tiles particularly managed in this console? Well, there’s a total of <strong>656 KB of VRAM</strong> available, and this chunk is split into different banks: Four 128 KB, one 64 KB, one 32 KB and three 16 KB. Programmers are free to fill the banks with drawings and then point the engine where the required data is. Both engines can read from any of these banks, but they can’t access the same one concurrently.</p><p>Nonetheless, there are some limitations on how data can be distributed. For instance, the ARM7 can only access two 128 KB banks. At the same time, these two banks can’t store sprites, and ‘sub’ is the only one capable of accessing the last 16 KB bank. The list goes on… but you get the idea.</p><p>One last thing, the 3D engine, which we will discuss later on, will access some of these banks to fetch textures.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-2-background-types">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-2-background-types"><h4 id="tab-2-2-background-types" class="tab-title">Background types</h4><p>Since the days of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/super-nintendo/#graphics">Super Nintendo</a>, the PPU has been leaning towards providing more flexibility for building background layers. 14 years later, we found ourselves with a chip that can fetch tiles and apply many <strong>affine transformations</strong> and if that wasn’t enough, the layer can be ultimately built from a frame buffer.</p><p>Before we discuss the different modes the 2D engine can operate to generate backgrounds, let me show you this list which specifies the types of backgrounds the engine can generate:</p><ul><li><strong>Character type group</strong>: These background types follow the traditional tile system, the frame is rendered by filling it with tiles.<ul><li><strong>Static</strong> or ‘Text’ background: An ordinary background. Up to 512x512 pixels wide, 256 colours and 16 palettes. It includes all the typical <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/super-nintendo/#tab-1-2-background">effects</a> (H/V flipping, H/V scrolling, mosaic, alpha blending) plus an extra ‘fading’ effect. Up to 1024 tiles can be used.</li><li><strong>Affine</strong> background: A background with <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/super-nintendo/#that-feature">affine transformations</a>. However, it doesn’t allow H/V flipping and can only fetch 256 tiles (one quarter from the maximum). The size of this layer is 1024x1024 pixels wide.</li><li><strong>Affine Extended - Character</strong>: Same as affine but restores the full amount of tiles and supports H/V flip.</li></ul></li><li><strong>Bitmap type group</strong>: Instead of processing tiles, the engine treats VRAM as a frame buffer.<ul><li><strong>Affine Extended - 256 colours</strong>: Inherit all the effects available from the ‘Affine Extended - Character’. The difference is that they are applied on a single 512x512 px bitmap.</li><li><strong>Affine Extended - Direct colour</strong>: Similar to the previous one but the frame buffer now supports up to 32,768 colours (15-bit).</li><li><strong>Large screen</strong>: Eats up a whole 128 KB chunk of VRAM to render a large 1024x512 px frame-buffer.</li></ul></li><li><strong>3D background</strong>: Displays the rendering of the 3D engine as a background layer, which is essential to show whatever the 3D engine has processed. While it doesn’t provide a lot of 2D effects, there’re interesting features like horizontal scrolling and alpha blending (with other background layers). Also, it’s the only type that supports up to 262,144 colours (18-bit)</li></ul><p>These modes can’t be chosen arbitrarily, instead, the console provides a series of <strong>background modes</strong> with different combinations set. Nevertheless, you can see here that the Affine Extended mode is available in three different flavours (‘Character’, ‘256 colours’ and ‘Direct colour’). So, in the next section, when you see that X background mode supports the ‘Affine Extended’ type, developers can choose which variant they want.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-1-tiles">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-3-background-modes">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-3-background-modes"><h4 id="tab-2-3-background-modes" class="tab-title">Background modes</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side pixel"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-1-1-layer-0-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-1-1-layer-0">Layer 0</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-2-layer-2-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-2-layer-2">Layer 2</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-3-layer-3-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-3-layer-3">Layer 3</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-1-1-layer-0"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/bg1.9c782df96fc338c8dfb1a1f95c425edeaaf768ef59688480a6aad58ea99c26ef.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/bg1.9c782df96fc338c8dfb1a1f95c425edeaaf768ef59688480a6aad58ea99c26ef.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Background Layer 0 (BG0). This particular layer will be shifted horizontally at certain scan lines to simulate the clouds moving.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-1-2-layer-2"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/bg2.4130751330c73853da1a8979fdd4e57812b004d54267be3e37d31efae464634c.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/bg2.4130751330c73853da1a8979fdd4e57812b004d54267be3e37d31efae464634c.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Background Layer 2 (BG2).</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-1-3-layer-3"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/bg3.cf5b5f3aceb7e5d307a23c9529ab8652c4c633bbacb5b0001b3d57316a0da81f.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/bg3.cf5b5f3aceb7e5d307a23c9529ab8652c4c633bbacb5b0001b3d57316a0da81f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Background Layer 3 (BG3).</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Static Background layers in use.</figcaption></figure><p>Here the background types are put into action. ‘Main’ and ‘Sub’ provide multiple modes of operation. All of them generate <strong>four background layers</strong>, however, each layer will have different capabilities depending on the mode activated:</p><ul><li><strong>Mode 0</strong>: 4 Static layers.</li><li><strong>Mode 1</strong>: 3 Static layers + 1 Affine layer.</li><li><strong>Mode 2</strong>: 2 Static layers + 2 Affine layers.</li><li><strong>Mode 3</strong>: 3 Static layers + 1 Affine Extended layer.</li><li><strong>Mode 4</strong>: 2 Static layers + 1 Affine layer + 1 Affine Extended layer.</li><li><strong>Mode 5</strong>: 2 Static layers + 2 Affine Extended layers.<ul><li>This is the most common mode used since it’s incredibly flexible.</li></ul></li><li><strong>Mode 6</strong>: 1 3D background layer + 1 Large screen.<ul><li>Since there is only space for a single frame buffer, this mode is only available on ‘Main’.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Additionally, in Mode 0 to 5, the ‘Main’ engine can use the first static layer as a 3D background instead. The 3D capabilities will be discussed later on.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-2-background-types">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-4-sprites">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-4-sprites"><h4 id="tab-2-4-sprites" class="tab-title">Sprites</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/sprites.774e46b73df7624ca335fa85206c5d1e92109d4ed1af89eba9dc36c124f99cfd.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/sprites.774e46b73df7624ca335fa85206c5d1e92109d4ed1af89eba9dc36c124f99cfd.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Rendered Sprite layer.</figcaption></figure><p>Sprites or ‘Objects’ inherit the same functionality from the GBA’s PPU, but we have two considerable additions.</p><p>Firstly, OAM (the region where sprites entries are stored) is now <strong>2 KB</strong> wide, enabling to display up to 128 sprites per frame per screen. Thus, 1 KB is allocated per engine.</p><p>Secondly, OAM can now reference <strong>bitmaps from VRAM</strong> as opposed to only using tiles and palettes. This is another departure from the tiling system. In fact, both sprite ‘modes’ can coexist in the same frame, since this option is set on each individual sprite.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-3-background-modes">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-5-result">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-5-result"><h4 id="tab-2-5-result" class="tab-title">Result</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/halfcomplete.35e87954aaa91b151ba44afff3f8b8c2de2bad4a3d557fa4b3889a614bad7fec.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/halfcomplete.35e87954aaa91b151ba44afff3f8b8c2de2bad4a3d557fa4b3889a614bad7fec.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">All layers merged… is there something missing?</figcaption></figure><p>As each layer renders on-the-fly, the final stage is tasked with merging everything and sending it to the selected screen. This is pretty much what happens with previous PPU-based consoles, does that mean we are done here?</p><p>Not yet! ‘Main’ still has to fetch a layer from another engine, the most powerful one.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-4-sprites">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="the-3d-accelerator">The 3D accelerator</h3><p>If you played with a Nintendo DS before, you know by now that this console can display a <em>particular</em> amount of 3D graphics. Unlike some GBA games, these aren’t processed by the CPU. Instead, CPU-NTR includes <strong>two components</strong> that compose the <strong>3D engine</strong>. Curiously enough, the design Nintendo applied reminds me of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#graphics">SGI’s RCP</a>.</p><p>Revisiting the ‘Background modes’ section, you’ll notice every mode has at least one static background, this is because you can fill that layer with graphics produced by the 3D engine. The only caveat is that only the ‘Main’ can do this, hence one of the reasons Mode 6 is only available for ‘Main’.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-3-1-geometry-engine-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-3-1-geometry-engine">Geometry Engine</a></li><li id="tab-3-2-rendering-engine-link"><a href="#tab-3-2-rendering-engine">Rendering Engine</a></li><li id="tab-3-3-result-link"><a href="#tab-3-3-result">Result</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-3-1-geometry-engine"><h4 id="tab-3-1-geometry-engine" class="tab-title">Geometry Engine</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/gpu/geometry.7ea6a7b7e3921c6f9f70cc0f1c57a606541ad6dbf106c5e9dc09bd1dfa109b3d.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="686" height="468" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/gpu/geometry.7ea6a7b7e3921c6f9f70cc0f1c57a606541ad6dbf106c5e9dc09bd1dfa109b3d.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Architecture of the Geometry Engine.</figcaption></figure><p>If you read any of the articles from the 5th or 6th generation, you may be wondering… Where’s the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/sega-saturn/#graphics">SIMD processor</a>? That’s a good question because the ARM9 is not particularly good at vector operations and I don’t think the dedicated divider is enough. That’s why Nintendo embedded a component called <strong>Geometry Engine</strong> that takes care of <strong>vertex transformations</strong>, <strong>projection</strong>, <strong>lighting</strong>, <strong>clipping</strong>, <strong>culling</strong> and <strong>polygon sorting</strong>, the latter is essential to properly use the transparency features.</p><p>This engine has some strict limitations, specifically the count of polygons it can process: There’s an extra <strong>248 KB of RAM</strong> available used to store processed geometry, this amount accounts for up to <strong>2048 triangles or 1706 quadrilaterals</strong>, although this limit is reduced by using polygon strips (as opposed to individual polys). To get a sense of this number, I suggest checking out the ‘interactive models’ sections in previous articles, you’ll see that it’s a concerning constraint, but don’t forget that the screen resolution of this console is also much smaller… so that compensates a bit.</p><p>Anyway, this engine is commanded using a <strong>Command FIFO</strong> which is filled with data from the CPU or DMA. The FIFO stores 256 entries, yet it’s complemented by another buffer called <strong>PIPE</strong> that stores four more commands (giving a total of 260).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-2-rendering-engine">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-2-rendering-engine"><h4 id="tab-3-2-rendering-engine" class="tab-title">Rendering Engine</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/gpu/rendering.54a52b753650a49a0027b474fd9e7adb152503b89a9e515e0d9dcdc60d9f4f4e.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="652" height="607" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/_diagrams/gpu/rendering.54a52b753650a49a0027b474fd9e7adb152503b89a9e515e0d9dcdc60d9f4f4e.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The architecture of the Rendering Engine.</figcaption></figure><p>The rendering engine is in charge of converting vectors to pixels (rasterising), colouring them (texture mapping) and applying lighting and other effects. It relies on <strong>perspective correction</strong> and <strong>Gouraud shading</strong> for interpolating textures and light, respectively. Moreover, the unit provides modern features like <strong>fog</strong>, <strong>alpha blending</strong>, <strong>depth buffering</strong> (either <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#modern-visible-surface-determination">Z-buffering</a> or a variant called W-buffering), <strong>stencil tests</strong> and <strong>anti-aliasing</strong>. However, the latter is very primitive (it just sets the outer edges of polygons as transparent) and it only works with opaque pixels.</p><p>The rendering system is a mix of old and new: Instead of rendering to a frame buffer, it employs <strong>line buffer rendering</strong>, where it fills scan lines (similarly to the 2D engine) and stores the results in a smaller buffer. This is because the 3D engine must work at pace with the 2D drawer.</p><p>Without the traditional frame buffer, the rasteriser employs <strong>scan-line rendering</strong>, traversing each scan-line to process polygon edges found within. Arisotura (the developer of MelonDS emulator) reported that for each quadrangle, the renderer can only fill <strong>one span per scan-line</strong> <sup id="bibref:11"><a href="#bib:graphics-arisotura" role="doc-biblioref">[11]</a></sup>. This can be a bit troubling, since the result will get messy if the quad is concave or has crossed edges, for instance.</p><p>Regarding effects, the unit also provides <strong>shadowing</strong> and a distinct feature called <strong>Toon Shading</strong> (another name for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#creativity">Cel Shading</a>): Even though this unit is not <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#the-importance-of-programmability">programmable</a>, the lighting parameters can be altered to achieve a cartoony effect.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-1-geometry-engine">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-3-result">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-3-result"><h4 id="tab-3-3-result" class="tab-title">Result</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/complete.ad64c1f4bb4e348934057c8f4809801019adc8e0ad46312f00c17fd40c24b475.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/mario/complete.ad64c1f4bb4e348934057c8f4809801019adc8e0ad46312f00c17fd40c24b475.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Ah, that’s more like it.</figcaption></figure><p>Instead of writing the results back to a frame buffer for display, the rendering engine will write to a block called <strong>Colour Buffer</strong> which stores up to 48 scan lines. Each scan line is fetched by the 2D engine to fill the BG0 layer in a FIFO manner.</p><p>3D rendering starts before the 2D one, enabling the latter to apply transformations on the new layer if required. ‘Main’ also allows to capture the 2D, 3D or combined frame generated, blend it with another frame in VRAM and write the result back to VRAM, which can be displayed afterwards.</p><p>In terms of control, the rendering engine also allows altering its parameters during mid-frame, due to employing a mechanism based on double-buffering that keeps a copy of the old state until the current frame finishes being drawn. Thus, no tearing will appear.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-2-rendering-engine">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="famous-comparisons">Famous comparisons</h3><p>Some of the first games released for this console attempt to resemble the ones from another console (namely, the Nintendo 64). So I wanted to give a quick summary of why players may see some substantial differences between the two versions:</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-4-1-first-example-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-4-1-first-example">First example</a></li><li id="tab-4-2-second-example-link"><a href="#tab-4-2-second-example">Second example</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-4-1-first-example"><h4 id="tab-4-1-first-example" class="tab-title">First example</h4><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft pixel"><a class="toleft pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/mario_n64.16b62d1c1169c59c490cefeb23d3679b776b1f10896e2c9ebb79a1e15cadf4f8.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/mario_n64.16b62d1c1169c59c490cefeb23d3679b776b1f10896e2c9ebb79a1e15cadf4f8_hu_34ee81d6b249a8ec.webp 320w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="320" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/mario_n64.16b62d1c1169c59c490cefeb23d3679b776b1f10896e2c9ebb79a1e15cadf4f8.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Super Mario 64 (1996).<br>Rendered at 320×240 pixels.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright pixel"><a class="toright pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/mario_nds.04fb4ba2c7f403a3b9f80621b69aa0a7a1598d69fa48595b0bc5a7edb9974474.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/mario_nds.04fb4ba2c7f403a3b9f80621b69aa0a7a1598d69fa48595b0bc5a7edb9974474.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Super Mario 64 DS (2004).<br>Rendered at 256x192 pixels.</figcaption></figure></div><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-4-2-second-example">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-4-2-second-example"><h4 id="tab-4-2-second-example" class="tab-title">Second example</h4><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft pixel"><a class="toleft pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/kart_n64.61e7d61169033127a969fbcb9dd34e8c3f3fdc47ef63675884d8a067aa71bdf0.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="320" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/kart_n64.61e7d61169033127a969fbcb9dd34e8c3f3fdc47ef63675884d8a067aa71bdf0.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Mario Kart 64 (1996).<br>Rendered at 320×240 pixels.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright pixel"><a class="toright pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/kart_nds.c9910fb86a35fc4ceae49f36f1ead5435a69c3b600f065f08c1a6a8c8aa7e41f.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="192" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/comparison/kart_nds.c9910fb86a35fc4ceae49f36f1ead5435a69c3b600f065f08c1a6a8c8aa7e41f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Mario Kart DS (2005).<br>Rendered at 256x192 pixels.</figcaption></figure></div><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-4-1-first-example">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><p>So, to explain what’s happening here, I’ve organised the different explanations based on what some people said on forums:</p><ul><li>NDS’ textures look more <strong>blocky</strong> → The rendering engine does not employ any filter, so textures are interpolated using the ‘nearest neighbour’ approach.</li><li>NDS’ textures look <strong>richer</strong> → The rendering engine is not limited by a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#tab-3-2-texture-memory">4 KB TMEM</a>, there’s instead up to 512 KB of VRAM available (apart from compression mechanisms provided) so naturally more data can be loaded.</li><li>NDS’ models contain <strong>pixelated edges</strong> → NDS models are rendered at a lower resolution compared to the N64.</li><li>NDS’ textures look <strong>distorted</strong> when seen from a distance → The rasteriser operates <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#missing-units">fixed-point</a> coordinates. Low resolution and lack of mip-mapping also attribute to aliasing.</li></ul><p>That’s pretty much in a nutshell, for more specialised cases, you’ll have to dive deeper into both engines and possibly of it.</p><hr><h2 id="audio">Audio</h2><p>Most of the audio improvements focus on enhancing those PCM channels that the GBA <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#audio">featured</a>. We’ve seen before that GBA games ultimately prioritised software sequencing over the PSG, and the result was quite impressive.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nintendods/video_posters/window.de25ef748111575cd51255a2c0b4e1d27b4dbe6117225415ab7390450ae18685.jpg" preload="none" width="960" height="720" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nintendods/window.f6d130a028e73e0e5b7ad90c08ddd4cef6c2774c27d93d280055277d075ca586.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Last Window: The Secret of Cape West (2010). Showing mixed stereo output.</figcaption></figure><p>Consequently, the new audio system features a total of <strong>16 PCM channels</strong>, allowing to shift the mixing task to the hardware. PCM samples can either be <strong>8-bit</strong> (<em>GBA-style</em>), <strong>16-bit</strong> (optimal resolution) or <strong>ACPCM</strong> (compressed form). In any case, the mixer produces a stereo signal that can be played through the speaker (now stereo) or headphones. It can also write the resulting stereo data to WRAM, enabling the sub-processor (ARM7) to apply some effects such as reverb.</p></div><p>With all being said, does this mean that the Nintendo DS can finally play encoded music (i.e. MP3)? It’s possible (in fact, a lot of homebrew programs implemented some form of it), but audio decoding takes up a lot of bandwidth and processing power <sup id="bibref:12"><a href="#bib:cpu-homebrew" role="doc-biblioref">[12]</a></sup>. So, audio sequencing still retains its place as the most feasible option.</p><h3 id="an-eccentric-psg-or-two">An eccentric PSG (or two)</h3><p>Since this console runs GBA games, it should then have something that reassembles the predecessor’s PSG (whether through hardware or software). Well, it so happens the last 6 channels contain a ‘PSG mode’ allowing any of them to synthesise either a pulse or a custom wave; and only two of them can create noise. But GBA games don’t use any of these!</p><p>You see, the mixer’s output frequency rate is <strong>32 kHz</strong> with a resolution of <strong>10-bit</strong> (considerably lower than the quality of the samples fed). Furthermore, <strong>it does not perform any form of interpolation</strong> to smooth out the loss of precision. These restrictions are not ideal for samples, as it adds noise. Though the actual perception of this phenomenon depends on your auditory capacity (I don’t notice the ‘hiss’ unless I boost the volume and compare it with a 16-bit version side-by-side), besides, it’s still a step forward coming from software-mixed samples with 8-bit resolution. Conversely, the aliasing effect is more problematic with PSG sounds, as downsampling the signal may introduce erroneous harmonics which distorts the original PSG tone. Nevertheless, games like New Super Mario Bros. happily make use of pulse waves for accompaniment, so I wouldn’t consider the PSG completely useless.</p><p>Back on topic, how does a GBA game handle all of this? <em>It doesn’t</em>, Nintendo fitted a <strong>separate sound system</strong> (within the same enclosure) for GBA mode that includes its own channels and mixer that follows the specifications of the predecessor. This way, GBA games won’t be affected by the new mixer’s limitations. Unfortunately, since this subsystem is segregated from the DS one (in other words, it doesn’t output to the DS’s mixer), DS games aren’t able to use it.</p><h3 id="interactive-comparison">Interactive comparison</h3><p>I’ve constructed this interactive widget that will allow you to compare how the new audio system affected the new generation of soundtracks. Each widget plays the same score but allows you to alternate between the old and new arrangements (I suggest wearing headphones to really notice the difference). Give it a whirl!</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><table class="audio-switcher" cellspacing="0"><tbody><tr id="_selection" class="audio-selector-group"><td audio="source1">GB Advance</td><td audio="source2">Nintendo DS</td></tr><tr class="audio-player-group"><td colspan="2"><audio controls="" controlslist="nodownload nofullscreen noplaybackrate noremoteplayback" class="active" loop=""><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/nintendods/trial_gba.cbe67e0a946bc05a721222469633107cee94fdb9a37197a26b53f2954892cfb8.ogg" type="audio/ogg" preload="metadata"><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/nintendods/trial_gba.9affd727da446b3381b2d0225d8058a13e8586f4341ced66b2959f2cd47b97df.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" preload="metadata">No support for audio.

Anyway, I hope you got a sense of how the sound subsystem has evolved.</p><h3 id="some-struggles">Some struggles</h3><p>Let me show you some tricky cases now, where the original console had some unique audio features that weren’t straightforward to recreate for this console, but I’ll let you be the judge of that:</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><table class="audio-switcher" cellspacing="0"><tbody><tr id="_selection" class="audio-selector-group"><td audio="source1">SNES</td><td audio="source2">Nintendo DS</td></tr><tr class="audio-player-group"><td colspan="2"><audio controls="" controlslist="nodownload nofullscreen noplaybackrate noremoteplayback" class="active" loop=""><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/nintendods/mario_snes.1c7558d5a2e276a077be11e660f494e2f8d4c5cf7caad23cbcc7dabaf715c3cd.ogg" type="audio/ogg" preload="metadata"><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/nintendods/mario_snes.2b491e53ba774286ade46efe204315b1884e9449907f88ee058f831363d78675.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" preload="metadata">No support for audio.
